items.title: El que subscribe certifico que este es el plano del terreno llamado las Mariposas que me fue concedido por el gobierno Mexicano : [Mariposa County, Calif.] / Juan B. Alvarado
items.credit: The Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley (Land Case Maps). Digitized via digicoll.lib.berkeley.edu. Public domain.
items.caption: Manuscript diseño (Mexican land-grant map), Mariposa County. From the U.S. private land-claim case files, The Bancroft Library.
items.headnote: This diseño of the floating grant Las Mariposas is certified by former governor Juan Bautista Alvarado, to whom the grant was made in 1844. Alvarado sold it to John C. Fremont in 1847, and it became extraordinarily valuable in the Gold Rush and the subject of the 1855 Supreme Court case Fremont v. United States.

items.headnote: Rancho Soscol (Suscol) was a very large grant of roughly 80,000 acres made to Mariano Guadalupe Vallejo around 1843-44, spanning lands near present Vallejo, Benicia, and the Napa River. The claim was ultimately rejected by the United States Supreme Court in 1862, a landmark ruling on the validity of Mexican grants.

items.title: Plano del terreno que pretende Don Estevan Smith : [Rancho Bodega, Calif.] / levantado por Jn. Vioget, 10 de Decembre 1843
items.credit: The Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley (Land Case Maps). Digitized via digicoll.lib.berkeley.edu. Public domain.
items.caption: Manuscript diseño (Mexican land-grant map), Sonoma County. From the U.S. private land-claim case files, The Bancroft Library.
items.headnote: This diseño, drawn by Jean Jacques Vioget in December 1843, accompanied Captain Stephen (Estevan) Smith's petition for Rancho Bodega on the Sonoma coast. Bodega Bay had served as the maritime port of the Russian-American Company's Fort Ross colony until the Russians withdrew in 1841, and the grant was formalized to Smith about 1844 under Governor Micheltorena. Smith is credited with introducing the first steam-powered sawmill to California.

items.headnote: Rancho Simi, formally San Jose de Nuestra Señora de Altagracia y Simi, was among the earliest and largest California grants, long held by the Pico family, and lay in present Ventura County. Its bounds covered well over 100,000 acres.
